exact_prompt:
I'm shopping for cottage cheese in the United States.

Is Good Culture cottage cheese worth paying more for than Daisy? Explain when you would choose each.
reviewed_answer:
Usually, yes—if you eat cottage cheese plain or use it as a creamy spread. Good Culture is generally richer, tangier, and thicker, while Daisy is the better value for a simple, traditional cottage cheese—especially if you’ll blend it into recipes or add toppings. Taste tests are split, so the premium is about texture and eating experience rather than a clear nutritional win.

Choose Good Culture when…

You eat it straight from the tub. Reviewers often praise its small, tender curds, pronounced tang, and thick, creamy texture; one recent taste test named its low-fat version best overall for flavor.

You want a spreadable texture. Consumer Reports found Good Culture’s organic 2% version best for spreading on toast, though it described the texture as dense—more ricotta-like than spoonable.

You prefer live active cultures and organic options. Good Culture’s products commonly emphasize live cultures and organic milk, which may matter to you if ingredient sourcing and fermentation are priorities.

You dislike watery cottage cheese. Its thicker consistency means less visible liquid pooling than many conventional brands.
drteresacrossley.substack

Choose Daisy when…

Price matters. Daisy is substantially cheaper; one comparison put Daisy around 17 cents per ounce versus Good Culture at 28 cents per ounce, so the premium can be meaningful over regular purchases.

You want a short, familiar ingredient list. Daisy is frequently noted for its simple ingredients and traditional curd-and-cream style.

You’re using it in smoothies, pancakes, lasagna, or blended sauces. Its more neutral, sour-cream-like flavor and distinct curds work well once mixed with other ingredients.

You like classic cottage cheese texture. Daisy has more separate curds and a thinner dressing; Consumer Reports rated its low-fat small-curd version among the top products overall, praising its balance of salt and milky sweetness.

Practical recommendation
Your use case	Better pick
Eating plain with fruit, honey, or pepper	Good Culture
Toast, bagels, or savory spreads	Good Culture
Smoothies, baking, sauces, lasagna	Daisy
Weekly high-volume protein snack	Daisy
You want organic / live-culture-forward options	Good Culture
You want the lowest-cost dependable staple	Daisy

For most people, I’d buy Daisy as the everyday tub and try Good Culture once to see whether its creamier, tangier profile justifies the upcharge for how you actually eat cottage cheese. If you mostly blend it or top it heavily, Daisy is probably the smarter buy; if you enjoy it unadorned, Good Culture is more likely to feel worth it.
